doc.title: Bobby Militello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

title: Accordion trio, fake books and discovering alternate blues changes
summary: In high school he learned changes by playing through fake books with an accordion trio, then worked out alternate chord substitutions at the piano.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: When did you start making a connection between the solos you were learning by ear and playing so well — the connection with the harmonies that were going on underneath.

Wow. I’d say sometime in high school. Maybe sophomore year, somewhere around there. There was a point where I was playing with an accordion trio. We were playing a lot of weddings and that kind of thing. The guy played chordovox, the organ type accordion, but before that regular accordion. And I used to like that, Art VanDamne and all those cats. I used to dig the sound. There was a fullness to it that I liked. So in any event, we were doing all these weddings and what we would do it get together on Thursdays, we’d practice for two hours and then watch “I Spy.” That was our routine every Thursday. So what we would do is open up a fake book, start reading every tune (there used to be three on a page in the old fake books) so you’d start reading and we’d play through every

single tune, just go through the A’s and the B’s and the C’s and the D’s, and then go back and start over again. Week after week. So that when we went to a job we could interpret these tunes that we didn’t know when somebody asked for them. So we could make them sound like something. And also, feeding the computer tunes. Inadvertently, by feeding the computer tunes you are also feeding it changes and finding out, oh, that’s the same as this. Oh, that’s the same as this. Oh that’s the same as this. Oh, that will work instead of that because it accomplishes the same — let’s say a two-five except different. It’s a different way to getting into the same one chord. Cool. All right we could do that on that tune. We could do this on that tune. Well I went home and I had gotten someone to donate a piano that I could have at the house. And I had a piano. And one day I’m playing blues changes and then I realized wait a minute, now wait a minute, you can do this and you can do that. And I started writing out all the alternate changes that I could play on the blues. And I realized at that point, wait a minute, just because it says C7 doesn’t mean I have to play a C7. There are a whole bunch of different things that I can play on that chord. That was my first revelation which got me to then Joey Azzorello, Azzorello, a great piano player—
